title: Aristotle's Physics
orientation: This chapter examines Aristotle's Physics and On the Heavens, the two treatises that, together, dominated Western science until Galileo. Russell reads them through their unstated 'imaginative background' -- the pre-theoretical picture of the world every philosopher works from -- and argues that Aristotle modeled physical motion on the behavior of living animals and the perceived Will of divine heavenly bodies, rather than on the mechanical picture that would eventually replace it. The chapter matters as a case study in how a scientifically false physics can nonetheless dominate a civilization's thought for nearly two thousand years, and in exactly which of its claims later science (Galileo, Newton) had to overturn.
historical_background: Russell stresses that both treatises 'dominated science until the time of Galileo,' and that terms like 'quintessence' and 'sublunary' still in use derive directly from their theories -- yet 'hardly a sentence in either can be accepted in the light of modern science.' He frames Aristotle's physics as reflecting a specifically Greek imaginative starting point: a world in which the two most salient kinds of motion are the self-caused movements of animals and the perfectly regular movements of heavenly bodies once widely worshipped as gods, very different from a modern student's starting image of machines, motor-cars, and aeroplanes.
philosophical_problems: What is the ultimate imaginative source of a philosopher's physical theories, beneath their formal, argued system?
What is 'nature' (phusis), and does it properly include purpose (an 'end') as well as material cause?
What is motion, and is a fixed distinction between a moving thing and a thing at rest even coherent?
Does time require a mind to count it, and did time (and motion) always exist?
What ultimately causes motion, and must the universe contain an unmoved first mover?
Is the heavenly, supralunary region made of different, eternal, incorruptible matter than the earthly, sublunary region?

philosophers_discussed.name: Aristotle
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Primary subject: Russell reconstructs the imaginative background, the teleological theory of nature, the theory of motion, the treatment of time, the argument for an unmoved mover, and the sublunary/supralunary cosmology of On the Heavens.

philosophers_discussed.name: Empedocles
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: His view that nature works of necessity, without purpose (an ancient anticipation of the survival of the fittest), is explicitly discussed and rejected by Aristotle, who argues that fixed, repeatable outcomes imply that preceding steps occur 'for the sake of' that outcome.

philosophers_discussed.name: Leucippus and Democritus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Their doctrine of the void is explicitly rejected by Aristotle in the Physics.

philosophers_discussed.name: Galileo
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited (looking ahead) as the scientist whose discoveries -- that projectiles move in parabolas, and the principle later formalized as Newton's First Law -- directly overturned core claims of Aristotelian physics.

core_concepts.name: The imaginative background of physics: Will as the source of motion
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Every philosopher, beneath their formal theory, has a simpler picture of how the world 'basically' works; for Aristotle and most Greeks, since the two most obviously self-moving things were animals and the heavenly bodies, the natural assumption was that all motion ultimately traces back to some kind of Will -- the capricious will of animals and humans on earth, the perfect, orderly will of a Divine Being in the heavens.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's own interpretive thesis (borrowing Santayana's phrase 'animal faith') that beneath Aristotle's explicit physical doctrines lies an unstated, pre-theoretical picture in which motion is modeled on animal self-movement and the willed regularity of divinized heavenly bodies, rather than on the strictly mechanical picture of later physics.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It explains, for Russell, why Aristotle's physics assimilates inanimate motion to purposive, quasi-biological behavior, and why this made his physics an obstacle rather than an aid to the eventual mechanical, mathematical physics of Galileo and Newton.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Russell's own diagnostic framework, applied to Aristotle but stated as a general claim about all philosophers' unstated 'crude' systems.
examples: A modern child distinguishes live animals from other things by their capacity for self-movement; Russell suggests this same childhood intuition, generalized by Aristotle into an adult theory, became the basis of his physics.
Anaxagoras was prosecuted for impiety for denying the sun and moon were alive -- showing how deeply the divinity of heavenly bodies was assumed in Greek culture.
competing_positions: The modern, mechanical imaginative background (motor-cars, aeroplanes, machines) in which 'animals have lost their importance' as models for lifeless motion.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Rooted in the widespread Greek religious assumption, instilled in childhood, that the sun and moon are gods.

core_concepts.name: Nature (phusis) as teleological
core_concepts.plain_explanation: For Aristotle, the 'nature' of a thing is its end or purpose -- what it is 'for,' the way it is the nature of an acorn to grow into an oak -- and things that have an internal source of their own motion or growth (animals, plants, the elements) are said to exist 'by nature.'
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's technical concept of phusis as a thing's end (that for the sake of which it exists), applied to whatever possesses an internal principle of motion or rest (broadly construed to include qualitative and quantitative change, not just locomotion), with a thing being 'more what it is' the closer it approaches its fulfilled, actualized form.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell judges this teleological conception, though well suited to explaining biological growth, to have become 'a great obstacle to the progress of science, and a source of much that was bad in ethics,' since it encourages treating 'natural' as automatically good and 'unnatural' as automatically blameworthy.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Suggested, Russell notes, by biological observation -- the acorn is 'potentially' an oak.
examples: 'The "nature" of a thing, Aristotle says, is its end, that for the sake of which it exists.'
objections: Russell notes this teleological framing directly gave rise to a moralized use of 'unnatural' to express blame, a usage he treats as still philosophically and ethically harmful in his own time.
competing_positions: Empedocles's view (rejected by Aristotle) that nature works of necessity, without purpose.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Persisted in ethical argument (appeals to what is 'natural' or 'unnatural') long after being abandoned in physics.

core_concepts.name: Motion as the actualization of potential
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle defines motion as 'the fulfilling of what exists potentially' -- so when a dog seizes a bone, the dog is fulfilling its nature by moving, while the bone is treated as simply staying still until seized -- but this picture cannot be squared with the fact that motion is really relative: if A moves relative to B, B equally moves relative to A.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's account of motion (kinesis) as the process by which a potentially existing state becomes actual, a definition that presupposes an absolute, non-relative distinction between a moving thing and a thing at rest, incompatible with the principle (basic to later physics) that locomotion can only be described relative to some reference body.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell singles this out as a definition that 'cannot be applied to dead matter' and, for the purposes of scientific physics, cannot be reconciled with treating all motion as strictly relative -- a foundational problem inherited from the whole 'nature as purpose' framework.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Follows directly from the teleological conception of nature.
examples: When a dog seizes a bone, common sense says the dog moves while the bone stays at rest 'until seized,' and that the motion serves a purpose (fulfilling the dog's nature) -- a picture that, Russell notes, cannot be extended to inanimate matter.
objections: Russell: 'no conception of an "end" is useful' for scientific physics, 'nor can any motion, in scientific strictness, be treated as other than relative.'
competing_positions: The relativistic conception of motion basic to post-Galilean and, ultimately, Einsteinian physics.

core_concepts.name: Time as numbered motion
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Aristotle argues time is not nothing (though it is made of a no-longer-existing past and a not-yet-existing future), but rather 'motion that admits of numeration' -- and, curiously, he wonders whether time could exist at all without a soul present to do the counting.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's account of time (in the Physics) as a countable aspect of motion, raising the puzzle of whether time can exist independently of a mind capable of numeration, since counting seems to require a counter; Aristotle also holds that motion, and hence time, has always existed and always will, in explicit disagreement with Plato, who held time was created.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It set up a direct point of conflict for later Christian Aristotelians, who were obliged to dissent from Aristotle's eternal-universe view since scripture holds that the universe had a beginning.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in the Physics, following the discussion of motion and preceding the argument for an unmoved mover.
examples: 'There always has been motion, and there always will be; for there cannot be time without motion, and all are agreed that time is uncreated, except Plato.'
competing_positions: Plato's view (noted as the sole exception among ancient philosophers) that time was created.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Created a direct doctrinal conflict for medieval Christian Aristotelians, who had to reject Aristotle's eternal-universe doctrine on biblical grounds.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly conflicted with the Christian doctrine of a created, temporally finite universe.

core_concepts.name: The unmoved mover and circular motion
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The Physics ends by arguing that there must be a single unmoved mover, without parts or size, located at the outer edge of the universe, that directly causes the perfect, continuous, circular motion of the outermost heavenly sphere -- circular motion being, for Aristotle, the one kind of motion capable of continuing forever.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Aristotle's conclusion (cross-referenced by Russell to the parallel argument in the Metaphysics) that there exists exactly one unmoved mover, lacking parts or magnitude and situated at the world's circumference, which directly causes the primary and only continuous, infinite kind of motion: uniform circular motion.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This argument forms the hinge between the Physics and On the Heavens, and supplied medieval theology with philosophical grounds for identifying the unmoved mover with God as the ultimate cause of cosmic motion.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed at the close of the Physics; treated by Russell as continuous with the parallel argument already discussed in connection with the Metaphysics.
objections: Russell later notes this whole framework is incompatible with Newton's First Law of Motion, since circular motion, involving continual change of direction, in fact requires a continually applied force (as in gravitation), rather than being 'natural' and self-sustaining as Aristotle assumed.
competing_positions: Newton's law of inertia and law of gravitation, which explain circular motion as requiring a centripetal force rather than being an uncaused 'natural' motion.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Provided a key philosophical resource for medieval natural theology's arguments for God's existence as the first cause of motion.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Later identified by Christian philosophers with God as the ultimate cause of cosmic motion.

core_concepts.name: Sublunary versus supralunary cosmology (the fifth element)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Everything below the moon (the sublunary sphere) is made of the four familiar elements -- earth, water, air, fire -- and is subject to generation and decay; everything from the moon outward is made of a fifth, perfect element ('quintessence') that never comes into being or passes away, and whose natural motion is circular rather than the up-and-down motion of the terrestrial elements.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The cosmology of On the Heavens, dividing the universe into a corruptible sublunary region composed of the four terrestrial elements (whose natural motions are rectilinear: fire and air upward, earth and water downward, in proportion to relative 'lightness' and 'heaviness') and an eternal, incorruptible supralunary region composed of a fifth element, whose only natural motion is perfect circular rotation, carrying the stars and planets on attached spheres.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This cosmology dominated Western astronomy and physics until Galileo, and directly generated the later terms 'quintessence' and 'sublunary'; Russell notes its poetic afterlife in Dante's Paradiso.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out in On the Heavens as the direct continuation of the Physics's argument for an unmoved mover causing circular motion.
examples: Comets were classified as sublunary (destructible) phenomena on this theory, since they appear and disappear -- a classification later overturned when seventeenth-century astronomers showed comets orbit the sun and are rarely as near as the moon.
objections: Russell: 'nothing in the visible world is exempt from change and decay'; stars and the sun are born from nebulae and eventually explode or die of cold, so the doctrine of eternal, incorruptible heavenly bodies has had to be abandoned entirely, a view Russell calls 'a product of the pagan worship of sun and moon and planets.'
competing_positions: Modern astrophysics, in which all matter, terrestrial and celestial, is subject to the same physical laws and processes of change.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly shaped medieval astronomy and cosmology, and the associated vocabulary ('quintessence,' 'sublunary') long outlived the theory itself.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Russell traces the belief in eternal, incorruptible heavenly bodies to the pagan worship of the sun, moon, and planets as gods.

arguments.title: Aristotle's teleological argument against Empedocles's proto-Darwinian view
premises: Empedocles held that natural processes occur of necessity, without purpose (an early version of survival of the fittest).
But things happen in fixed, repeatable ways.
When a series of events has a completion (an end-state), Aristotle argues, the preceding steps occur 'for the sake of' that completion.
arguments.conclusion: Nature cannot work by blind necessity alone; the fixed, repeated patterns of natural process show that things which 'by a continuous movement originated from an internal principle, arrive at some completion' are properly called natural, and natural processes are for the sake of their outcomes.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as Aristotle's explicit rejection, within the Physics, of a view he finds in Empedocles that anticipates the modern theory of natural selection -- Aristotle insists instead on purpose (teleology) as a genuine causal category in nature.
objections: Russell judges this whole conception, though 'admirably suited to explain the growth of animals and plants,' to have become 'a great obstacle to the progress of science' once generalized to all of nature, including inanimate matter.
implications: Committed Western physics, for nearly two thousand years, to explaining natural processes by their purposes or ends rather than by efficient, mechanical causes -- an approach only reversed at length by the scientific revolution.

arguments.title: Russell's incompatibility argument: Aristotelian 'natural' circular motion versus Newton's First Law
premises: Aristotle holds that circular motion is the 'natural,' self-sustaining motion of the heavenly bodies, requiring no external cause to continue.
Newton's First Law states that a body in motion continues in a straight line at uniform velocity unless acted on by an external force.
Circular motion involves continual change of direction.
arguments.conclusion: Aristotelian physics, in which circular celestial motion is uncaused and 'natural,' is directly incompatible with Newtonian physics, in which circular motion requires a continually applied force (such as gravitation) directed toward the center.
arguments.explanation: Russell uses this contrast to make explicit exactly what the scientific revolution had to overturn in Aristotle's cosmology: not simply particular factual errors, but the entire framework in which circular motion could be treated as requiring no cause at all.
implications: Demonstrates why On the Heavens's entire supralunary cosmology, resting on 'natural' uncaused circular motion, could not survive the adoption of Newtonian mechanics.

key_distinctions: A philosopher's explicit, formal system vs. their unstated 'imaginative background' (Santayana's 'animal faith')
Existing 'by nature' (having an internal principle of motion: animals, plants, elements) vs. existing from other, external causes
Motion in Aristotle's wide sense (including qualitative and quantitative change) vs. mere locomotion
The sublunary sphere (four elements, generation and decay, rectilinear motion) vs. the supralunary sphere (fifth element, eternal and incorruptible, circular motion)
'Natural,' uncaused circular motion (Aristotle) vs. force-caused circular motion (Newton's gravitation)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell notes Aristotle explicitly engages and rejects Empedocles's proto-evolutionary account of nature working by necessity without purpose, and rejects the void as maintained by Leucippus and Democritus. He also contrasts Aristotle's teleological, animal-and-Will-centered imaginative background with the more purely mechanical outlook of 'a few men of genius such as Democritus and Archimedes,' who stood apart from the general Greek pattern.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell traces Aristotelian physics's long dominance down to Galileo, whose discovery that projectiles move in parabolas (not straight lines followed by sudden vertical fall) directly refuted Aristotle's account of terrestrial motion, and to Newton, whose First Law of Motion and law of gravitation are shown to be fundamentally incompatible with Aristotle's doctrine of 'natural,' uncaused circular motion. He also notes the enduring poetic influence of the sublunary/supralunary cosmology on Dante's Paradiso, and observes that Copernicus, Kepler, and Galileo all had to combat Aristotelian authority (alongside, in Galileo's case, biblical authority) to establish a heliocentric universe.
religion_science_culture_context: Russell connects Aristotle's physics directly to the religious culture that produced it: the assumption that heavenly bodies are divine (with Anaxagoras's prosecution for impiety as evidence of how seriously this was held), and the eventual eclipse of belief in eternal, incorruptible heavenly bodies, which Russell calls 'a product of the pagan worship of sun and moon and planets.' He also notes the durable linguistic legacy of Aristotle's cosmology in the still-current terms 'quintessence' and 'sublunary.'
russell_presentation: Russell opens with a methodological reflection of his own -- that every philosopher has both a formal system and a cruder, unstated 'imaginative background,' and that Aristotle's background modeled all motion on animal self-movement and divine celestial Will, in contrast to a modern, machine-centered imagination. He then works through the Physics's central doctrines in sequence: 'nature' (phusis) as end or purpose; the classification of things existing 'by nature'; Aristotle's explicit rejection of Empedocles's necessity-without-purpose view; the definition of motion as actualization of potential, and its incompatibility with the relativity of motion; the rejection of the void; the treatment of time as numbered motion, including the puzzle of time's dependence on a counting soul; and the argument, closing the Physics, for a single unmoved mover causing eternal circular motion. He then turns to On the Heavens and its sublunary/supralunary cosmology, the four terrestrial elements and the fifth celestial element, before closing with a review of the specific later scientific discoveries (comets' true orbits, Galileo's parabolic projectiles, Newton's First Law, the non-eternity of stars) that overturned each major claim in turn.
critical_context: Russell explicitly and repeatedly measures Aristotle's physics against the physics that replaced it, treating this comparison as the chapter's main critical payload rather than adding a separate closing verdict: the definition of motion fails once the relativity of motion is recognized; the doctrine of 'natural,' uncaused circular motion is incompatible with Newton's First Law and law of gravitation; and the doctrine of eternal, incorruptible heavenly bodies has had to be abandoned given that stars are now known to be born from nebulae and eventually die. Russell frames the teleological conception of nature as having done positive damage beyond physics as well, calling it 'a source of much that was bad in ethics' through the moralized use of 'unnatural' as automatically blameworthy -- a Layer 3 aside about the doctrine's afterlife outside science.
key_takeaways: Aristotle's Physics and On the Heavens dominated Western science until Galileo, leaving a permanent linguistic legacy ('quintessence,' 'sublunary') despite being almost entirely rejected by modern science.
Russell argues Aristotle's physics reflects an unstated 'imaginative background' modeling motion on animal self-movement and the Will of divinized heavenly bodies, rather than on mechanism.

Aristotle's teleological concept of 'nature' (phusis) as a thing's end explains growth well but became, per Russell, 'a great obstacle to the progress of science' once generalized to all natural process.
Aristotle's definition of motion as 'the fulfilling of what exists potentially' cannot be reconciled with the relativity of motion basic to later physics.

The Physics concludes with an argument for a single unmoved mover causing eternal circular motion, which On the Heavens elaborates into a sublunary (four elements, decay) versus supralunary (fifth element, eternal, circular) cosmology.

Later science overturned this cosmology point by point: comets are not sublunary, projectiles move in parabolas (Galileo) rather than Aristotle's rectilinear-then-vertical path, circular motion requires continual force (Newton) rather than being 'natural,' and heavenly bodies are not eternal but are born and eventually die.
study_notes:
Because this chapter is short, it works well read as a single sustained argument rather than a loose survey: Russell's opening methodological point (every physics has an unstated 'imaginative background') is not a throwaway remark but the interpretive key to everything that follows. Keep asking, as you read each Aristotelian doctrine, how it reflects the animal-movement/divine-Will picture Russell introduces at the start -- this makes doctrines like 'motion is the fulfilling of what exists potentially' and 'circular motion is natural for the heavens' feel much less arbitrary, even though Russell ultimately judges them false.

The chapter's second half is organized as a point-by-point scorecard against later science, and it is worth building your own table while reading: for each Aristotelian claim (comets are sublunary; projectiles move in straight lines then fall; circular motion is uncaused and 'natural'; heavenly bodies are eternal), note the specific later discovery (comet orbits; Galileo's parabolas; Newton's First Law and gravitation; stellar birth and death) that overturned it. This scorecard approach mirrors exactly how Russell structures his own closing paragraphs, and it is the fastest way to retain the chapter's content.

Finally, notice the aside about 'nature' and ethics: Russell flags, almost in passing, that the teleological concept of nature did lasting ethical damage by licensing the inference from 'unnatural' to 'bad' -- a use of the word that long outlived the physics that originally grounded it. This is a good example of how a scientific idea's afterlife can outrun its original scientific content.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Aristotle's word for 'nature,' closely tied to growth -- the 'nature' of an acorn is to grow into an oak.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's technical concept of a thing's end or telos, applied to whatever possesses an internal principle of motion, growth, or rest, distinguishing what exists 'by nature' from what exists through other, external causes.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Aristotle's proposed single, unchanging cause, without parts or size, that directly causes the eternal circular motion of the outermost heavens.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The single, partless, magnitude-less first cause of motion Aristotle argues for at the close of the Physics, directly causing the primary, continuous, infinite circular motion of the outermost celestial sphere.
related_concepts: The unmoved mover and circular motion

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The 'below the moon' region, where things are born and decay, versus the 'above the moon' region, where things (Aristotle believed) never change.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Aristotle's cosmological division, in On the Heavens, between the corruptible, four-element terrestrial region below the moon and the eternal, incorruptible, fifth-element celestial region from the moon outward.
related_concepts: Sublunary versus supralunary cosmology (the fifth element)

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The special, perfect substance Aristotle believed made up the stars and heavens, distinct from earth, water, air, and fire.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The fifth element of On the Heavens, composing the supralunary region, whose sole natural motion is uniform circular rotation, in contrast to the rectilinear natural motions of the four terrestrial elements.
related_concepts: Sublunary versus supralunary cosmology (the fifth element)

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that whether something is 'moving' only makes sense relative to something else -- there's no absolute fact about which of two things is really moving.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The principle, incompatible with Aristotle's definition of motion as actualization of potential, that locomotion can only be meaningfully described relative to a chosen reference body, since if A moves relative to B, B equally moves relative to A.
related_concepts: Motion as the actualization of potential

questions.prompt: What does Russell mean by a philosopher's 'imaginative background,' and what was Aristotle's, according to Russell?
questions.answer: The simpler, unstated picture of how the world basically works that underlies a philosopher's formal, argued system; for Aristotle, Russell argues it modeled all motion on animal self-movement and the Will of divinized heavenly bodies, rather than on mechanism.
questions.explanation: Russell borrows the phrase 'animal faith' from Santayana for this idea.

questions.prompt: How does Aristotle define the 'nature' (phusis) of a thing?
questions.answer: Its end -- that for the sake of which it exists -- giving the concept a teleological implication, as in the acorn's 'nature' being to grow into an oak.
questions.explanation: Russell judges this framework well suited to biology but harmful once generalized to all of physics and to ethics.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Aristotle's argument against Empedocles's view that nature works by necessity without purpose.
questions.answer: Things happen in fixed, repeatable ways; when a series has a completion, Aristotle argues, the preceding steps occur for the sake of that completion; therefore natural processes cannot be purposeless, but must involve an internal, teleological principle.
questions.explanation: Russell notes this rejects a view that anticipates the modern theory of natural selection.

questions.prompt: Why does Russell say Aristotle's definition of motion cannot be applied to 'dead matter' or accepted by scientific physics?
questions.answer: Because motion, in scientific strictness, must be treated as relative (if A moves relative to B, B moves relative to A), whereas Aristotle's definition (motion as fulfilling a purposive potential, as with a dog seizing a bone) presupposes an absolute distinction between the moving thing and the thing at rest.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's central critique of Aristotle's concept of motion.

questions.prompt: Contrast Aristotle's account of circular celestial motion with Newton's First Law of Motion.
questions.answer: Aristotle holds circular motion is 'natural' for the heavenly bodies and requires no external cause; Newton's First Law holds a body continues in a straight line at uniform velocity unless acted on by a force, so circular motion (a continual change of direction) requires a continually applied force, as in gravitation -- directly contradicting Aristotle's framework.
questions.explanation: Russell presents this as the key point of incompatibility between Aristotelian and Newtonian physics.

questions.prompt: What discovery about comets, and what discovery about projectile motion, overturned specific claims of Aristotelian physics?
questions.answer: Comets, classified as sublunary/destructible by Aristotle, were shown in the seventeenth century to orbit the sun and rarely come near the moon; and Galileo showed that projectiles move in parabolas, not (as Aristotelian physics held) in a straight line followed by a sudden vertical fall.
questions.explanation: Both examples appear in Russell's closing scorecard of Aristotelian claims overturned by later science.

quiz.prompt: Match each Aristotelian claim to the later discovery that overturned it: (1) comets are sublunary/destructible, (2) projectiles move in a straight line then fall vertically, (3) heavenly bodies are eternal and incorruptible.
options: (1) comets shown to orbit the sun, rarely near the moon; (2) Galileo showed projectiles move in parabolas; (3) stars shown to be born from nebulae and eventually die
(1) refuted by Newton's First Law; (2) refuted by Copernicus; (3) refuted by Kepler's ellipses
All three were refuted by the same single discovery
None of these claims were ever overturned
quiz.explanation: Each Aristotelian cosmological claim was overturned by a distinct later scientific discovery, as Russell's closing scorecard lays out.
quiz.related_concept: Sublunary versus supralunary cosmology (the fifth element)

quiz.prompt: Russell argues that Aristotle's teleological conception of 'nature' caused harm only in physics, not in ethics.
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly says the concept was 'a source of much that was bad in ethics,' via the moralized use of 'unnatural' as blameworthy.

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze Russell's concept of a philosopher's 'imaginative background,' using Aristotle's physics as the case study. How does the animal-movement/divine-Will picture explain specific doctrines in the Physics and On the Heavens?
rubric: Accurately explains the concept of 'imaginative background'
Connects it to at least two specific Aristotelian doctrines (e.g., teleological nature, natural circular motion)
Contrasts it with the modern mechanical imaginative background

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's point-by-point comparison of Aristotelian cosmology with the later discoveries (Galileo's parabolas, Newton's First Law, stellar birth and death) that overturned it. Does this comparison method fairly represent Aristotle's achievement, or does it risk judging ancient science unfairly by modern standards?
rubric: Accurately lists at least three specific overturned claims and their refutations
Considers whether comparing ancient and modern science by this method is fair
Addresses Russell's own historically sympathetic remarks elsewhere in the book
